Incomprehensibility of God
in-kom-pre-hen-si-BIL-i-tee of GOD
noun phrase (theology proper / divine attributes)
The doctrine that God, being infinite, cannot be fully comprehended (exhaustively known) by the finite creature, though He can be truly known as He reveals Himself. Grounded in the unsearchableness of God (Romans 11:33-34; Job 11:7; Isaiah 40:28; Psalm 145:3). Distinguished from agnosticism (which denies that God can be truly known at all).

Biblical Definition

The doctrine that God, being infinite, cannot be fully comprehended (exhaustively known) by the finite creature, though He can be truly known as He reveals Himself. The doctrine holds two truths in balance. (1) God cannot be exhaustively comprehended: the finite creature cannot fully grasp the infinite God; God's ways and being exceed the creature's comprehension. O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? (Romans 11:33-34); Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection? (Job 11:7); there is no searching of his understanding (Isaiah 40:28); his greatness is unsearchable (Psalm 145:3). (2) God can be truly (though not exhaustively) known: God has revealed Himself truly in His works, His Word, and supremely in His Son, so that the creature can have true (though not comprehensive) knowledge of God. This is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent (John 17:3); the knowledge of God is the goal of redemption (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11). The Reformed-confessional doctrine holds the substantive balance: God is incomprehensible (not exhaustively knowable by the finite creature) but truly knowable (genuinely revealed and apprehensible as He has made Himself known). The substantive theological implications: the incomprehensibility of God humbles the creature, guards against rationalist presumption (the attempt to comprehend God by autonomous reason), and grounds the necessity of revelation (we know God only as He reveals Himself); while the true knowability of God assures the believer that his knowledge of God, though not comprehensive, is genuine and saving. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine against both rationalism (which presumes to comprehend God exhaustively by reason) and agnosticism / mysticism (which denies that God can be truly known at all). God is incomprehensible yet truly knowable: the creature cannot fully comprehend the infinite God, but can truly know Him as He has revealed Himself in His Word and in His Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that God, being infinite, cannot be exhaustively comprehended by the finite creature, though He can be truly known as He reveals Himself; Romans 11:33-34 (how unsearchable are his judgments), Job 11:7, Isaiah 40:28; held against rationalism (presuming to comprehend God) and agnosticism (denying God can be truly known).

INCOMPREHENSIBILITY OF GOD, n. phr. (theology proper / divine attributes) God, being infinite, cannot be fully comprehended (exhaustively known) by the finite creature, though He can be truly known as He reveals Himself. Two truths in balance: (1) God cannot be exhaustively comprehended (Romans 11:33-34, how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out; Job 11:7; Isaiah 40:28; Psalm 145:3); (2) God can be truly (though not exhaustively) known (John 17:3, this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God; Jeremiah 31:34). The incomprehensibility humbles the creature, guards against rationalist presumption, grounds the necessity of revelation; the true knowability assures the believer of genuine saving knowledge. Held against rationalism and agnosticism/mysticism.

Key Scripture

Romans 11:33-34 — "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?"

Isaiah 40:28 — "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary? there is no searching of his understanding."

Deuteronomy 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

John 17:3 — "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."

Modern Corruption

The incomprehensibility of God is held against rationalism (which presumes to comprehend God exhaustively by autonomous reason) and agnosticism/mysticism (which denies that God can be truly known at all); God is incomprehensible yet truly knowable.

expand to see more

The incomprehensibility of God is held against two opposing errors. Rationalism presumes to comprehend God exhaustively by autonomous reason, subjecting God to the categories and judgments of the finite human mind; this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God's judgments are unsearchable and His ways past finding out (Romans 11:33-34), that no one has known the mind of the Lord or been His counselor (Romans 11:34; Isaiah 40:13-14). Agnosticism and certain forms of mysticism deny that God can be truly known at all, treating God as utterly unknowable, beyond all true predication (the radical apophaticism that says we can only know what God is not); this contradicts the biblical doctrine that God has revealed Himself truly and that knowing Him is eternal life (John 17:3). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional balance: God is incomprehensible (the finite creature cannot exhaustively comprehend the infinite God) yet truly knowable (God has revealed Himself genuinely in His works, His Word, and supremely in His Son, so that the creature can have true and saving knowledge of God). Deuteronomy 29:29 holds the balance perfectly: the secret things belong to the LORD (the incomprehensible depths beyond the creature's grasp), but the revealed things belong to us and to our children forever (the true knowledge God has graciously given). The believer adores the incomprehensible greatness of God while resting in the true knowledge of Him that God has revealed; he does not presume to comprehend the infinite God by reason, nor despair of knowing Him truly, but receives with humility and gratitude the true knowledge of God that the incomprehensible God has graciously revealed.

Hebrew Roots

Romans 11:33-34; Job 11:7; Isaiah 40:28; Deuteronomy 29:29; God incomprehensible (not exhaustively knowable) yet truly knowable (genuinely revealed); held against rationalism and agnosticism/mysticism.
